title: Rane’s Leadership Library
subtitle: A collection of the stories, mistakes, ideas, and books I want to keep returning to long after Trailblazers ends.

entries.title: Classmate Feedback
entries.principle: Cultivate Self-Awareness, Personal Agility & Growth
entries.left_note: At the beginning of the semester, I thought I was pretty self-aware. I knew I was driven, emotional, stubborn about my ideas, non-confrontational, and someone who cares a lot about doing things well. Trailblazers showed me there was more to it than knowing my own intentions.
entries.reflection: One of my classmates told me I could seem intimidating and unapproachable. It was hard to hear because it did not match who I am with people who know me well. It made me realize that I keep my more silly, open, caring side guarded at first. Since then, I have tried to start more conversations, ask people questions, and hear feedback without immediately explaining myself. I need to pay attention when my intent and my impact do not match and be thoughtful of my actions.

entries.title: AI Curriculum Activity
entries.context: Using the tool without losing my judgment
entries.principle: Cultivate Self-Awareness, Personal Agility & Growth
entries.left_note: I study Information Systems and AI Business Strategy, so I care about knowing how to use AI well. While I was building curriculum for the class I teach, I spent a lot of time trying to get AI to give me the perfect activity.
entries.reflection: The activity I had thought of from the beginning was better because I knew the students, where they were, and what would actually work in that room. AI did not have that context. It can help me organize, research, and get unstuck. It cannot make the call for me. I do not want to hand off the creative part of my work because a tool can make something faster.

entries.title: Ken Garff Scope
entries.context: Choosing the problem we could actually help solve
entries.principle: Actively Find & Formulate the Right Problems
entries.left_note: At the start of our Ken Garff for Good project, my team thought we could solve everything. We were talking about student motivation, school implementation, scholarships, career exploration, and more. There were so many directions that it became hard to tell what would really help.
entries.reflection: We finally narrowed our focus to the administrator experience. The question became: what would make rollout and ongoing use better for the people at schools who make the program possible? We do not have our final recommendation yet, but the project feels much clearer. I learned that strategy often means choosing a smaller, more specific problem instead of trying to make an idea cover everything.

entries.title: Blog Posts
entries.context: The internship I would approach differently now
entries.principle: Actively Find & Formulate the Right Problems
entries.left_note: During my Goff Explorers internship, I wrote SEO blog posts for a therapy center. At first, I treated the assignment like a weekly checklist. I picked a topic, wrote the blog, and moved on.
entries.reflection: When I brought an assignment to office hours, my professor pushed me to make a plan for the full semester and explain why each topic belonged in it. If I did it again, I would start with more questions about the audience, what people were searching for, and how the therapy center used content across newsletters and social media. I had completed the work. I had not thought enough about the result it was supposed to create.

entries.title: Disney Interview
entries.context: Talking about work that does not have one clear answer
entries.principle: Craft & Share a Compelling Vision
entries.left_note: Preparing for my Disney interview made me look back at Trailblazers differently. I had to explain a project that was still moving, with no obvious answer and a team that had to figure things out as we went.
entries.reflection: I realized I had a better story when I focused on the questions we asked and why the project mattered to schools and students. I was not trying to give a polished class-project answer. I could explain the uncertainty, the choices we made, and what we learned from narrowing our focus. Trailblazers gave me a real example of the kind of product work I want to do.

entries.title: Administrator Interviews
entries.context: Listening before deciding what help looks like
entries.principle: Craft & Share a Compelling Vision
entries.left_note: Trailblazers changed how I think about community impact. Caring about a cause and putting in effort are not enough if the work does not fit the people it is supposed to help.
entries.reflection: It would have been easy to make assumptions about why students do or do not feel ready for college. The administrator interviews kept bringing us back to the real workflows, time limits, and differences between schools. That is the kind of listening I want to bring to community work after college too. I do not want to wait until I have a bigger title or more free time before I contribute.

entries.title: DEA Demo
entries.context: Preparing for a high-stakes customer conversation
entries.principle: Deliver Results with Strong Personal Ownership
entries.left_note: During my Lucid internship, a sales demo for the DEA, our company’s largest government account, was accidentally assigned to me while my manager was away. Once my manager said he was comfortable with me continuing, I decided to take it seriously.
entries.reflection: I talked to customer success managers who knew the account, built a slide deck, practiced my five-minute pitch, and met with mentors and my manager. The demo went well. More importantly, I knew I had prepared for it myself. Ownership means being reliable when something important lands in front of me. It means doing what I can with the information and support I have.

entries.title: Workplan Version 2
entries.principle: Deliver Results with Strong Personal Ownership
entries.left_note: Our Trailblazers team struggled early on. We divided work poorly, disagreed often, and did not have clear roles. It was hard to tell who was taking initiative on what. Creating version two of our workplan was a turning point.
entries.reflection: The new workplan showed what each person was taking on, when it was happening, and how it fit into the project. That gave us a better way to talk about what was not working. I also had to admit I was part of the tension. I was so focused on solving the problem that I could become overbearing. When a team gets stuck, I need to ask more questions before I take over.

entries.title: Canva Graphics
entries.context: Using a skill my supervisor did not know I had
entries.principle: Identify & Align Resources to Generate Value
entries.left_note: While I was writing blog posts in Explorers, I realized my supervisor did not know I had started Rane Design Co. in high school or that I could make graphics in Canva. I asked if I could create visuals for each blog post.
entries.reflection: My supervisor was excited because the graphics could go in newsletters and make the posts easier to share. That changed how I saw the assignment. The blogs became part of a larger communication system. I learned to speak up about skills I already have instead of waiting for someone to guess what I can contribute.

entries.title: Lucid Office Hours
entries.context: Sharing product knowledge with sales reps
entries.principle: Identify & Align Resources to Generate Value
entries.left_note: At Lucid, I realized I could help sales reps with product knowledge and teaching. I started office hours where reps could ask questions, learn new features, and feel more confident talking with customers.
entries.reflection: Office hours were outside the original scope of my internship, but they felt useful. They also gave newer reps a place to ask questions without worrying that they were slowing everyone down. Explorers had already taught me to look beyond the first task I am assigned. That lesson made it easier to take this on at Lucid.

entries.title: Team Feedback
entries.context: Learning to think with people instead of around them
entries.principle: Maintain a Relentless Focus on Creating Value
entries.left_note: Trailblazers felt different from normal group work. In a lot of classes, people divide tasks, coordinate over text, and combine everything at the end. That did not work here because the direction was not obvious.
entries.reflection: We had to question each other’s ideas, talk through uncertainty, and understand why people were approaching the same problem differently. I can get attached to an idea when I think it is right. This project made me pay more attention to that. I want people I work with to feel like I helped them think clearly and contribute fully, not like I just pushed the project forward.

entries.title: Future Product Manager
entries.context: The kind of work I want to do
entries.principle: Maintain a Relentless Focus on Creating Value
entries.left_note: I want to be a product manager who stays close to the real problem and the people dealing with it. I care about succeeding, but I do not want career goals to crowd out creativity, mentorship, education access, or the causes I care about.
entries.reflection: My plan is to keep developing as a strategist, make time for the values that matter to me, and use technology in a way I can stand behind. I want to keep giving back through post-secondary education and mentorship. I am excited by AI and product work. I also want the work I choose to leave people and communities better than I found them.

entries.title: Leaving Basketball
entries.context: Knowing when a chapter has done its job
entries.principle: Cultivate Self-Awareness, Personal Agility & Growth
entries.left_note: Basketball was a huge part of my life for six years. I spent late nights working on free throws with my dad, went to leadership camps, and pushed myself hard enough to finally earn a varsity spot. Deciding not to play my senior year was not an easy decision.
entries.reflection: I was proud of the work ethic basketball gave me, but I also knew the environment was no longer helping me become the person I wanted to be. Leaving was not the same as quitting. It was a choice to make room for what came next. That experience taught me to be honest about when persistence is meaningful and when it is time to pivot.

entries.title: Softball Team Captain
entries.principle: Craft & Share a Compelling Vision
entries.left_note: I joined slowpitch softball because the team needed enough people to have a season. I had never held a mitt before, but after one year I became an All-Star shortstop and team captain. The part I cared about most was how the team felt to be on.
entries.reflection: When practices were not well prepared and teammates were discouraged, I looked for small ways to give the group more energy. I ran the team social media account and featured every teammate, not only the people who got the most attention. I learned that leadership can be practical and personal at the same time. People work harder when they feel like they belong to something and are noticed inside it.

entries.title: Rane Design Co.
entries.principle: Identify & Align Resources to Generate Value
entries.left_note: In middle school, I watched calligraphy and bullet-journaling videos for hours, practiced with brush pens, and eventually realized I could make something more from the skill. I opened Rane Design Co. and started selling calligraphy, vinyl projects, and design work.
entries.reflection: The first order was a four-dollar Valentine template I made for my little sister. It felt much bigger because it showed me I could take an interest, learn the tools, and build something people actually wanted. Later, I used that same skill for nonprofits, school groups, and community projects. I still come back to that lesson: creativity becomes more valuable when I connect it to a real person or need.

entries.title: Point Guard College
entries.context: Learning to lead before I felt ready
entries.principle: Deliver Results with Strong Personal Ownership
entries.left_note: At Point Guard College, I spent long days in the gym with players who were faster and more experienced than I was. I went to improve at basketball, but the lessons I kept were about communication, effort, and the effect one person can have on a team.
entries.reflection: I learned that I did not need to be the best player in the room to influence the energy of the room. I could communicate, hustle, encourage someone after a mistake, and show up prepared. Those are simple habits, but they became part of how I think about ownership. I still want to be the person who makes a team steadier when the pressure goes up.

entries.title: The Library Committee
entries.principle: Maintain a Relentless Focus on Creating Value
entries.left_note: For three years in middle school, I spent lunch in the library as part of the student purchasing committee. We researched new books, listened to pitches from local bookstores, and helped decide what would end up on the shelves.
entries.reflection: It was one of my earliest experiences seeing that a small decision can shape a shared space. We were not only choosing books we liked. We were helping create a library where other students could find a story that felt like it was meant for them. That is still the kind of value I want to create in my work: making a thoughtful choice that helps someone else feel included, understood, or more curious.

entries.title: The Enchantments
entries.context: Saying yes to a hard thing
entries.principle: Cultivate Self-Awareness, Personal Agility & Growth
entries.left_note: I did not think I was a hiking person. Then I trained for a three-day backpacking trip, finished twenty-eight miles with my group, and later took on the Enchantments, a twenty-four-mile day hike with my dad.
entries.reflection: The hike was exhausting and emotionally intense, but finishing changed the story I had been telling myself about what I could do. I learned that I like challenges that ask me to stay present, keep moving, and trust that effort adds up. It also reminded me not to decide too quickly that something is not for me just because I have not tried it yet.

entries.title: The Ride of a Lifetime
entries.principle: Craft & Share a Compelling Vision
entries.left_note: I read this while I was preparing for my Disney interview, and it became one of those books where I kept stopping to underline things. I have always loved Disney for the feeling it creates, but this helped me see the strategic choices underneath that feeling.
entries.reflection: Bob Iger had a clear idea of the experience Disney could create for people, and his decisions kept coming back to that. Reading it before my interview made me think about the kind of product work I am drawn to. I like work that gives people a feeling, while still having a clear reason behind every decision.

entries.title: Radical Candor
entries.principle: Cultivate Self-Awareness, Personal Agility & Growth
entries.left_note: This one feels a little too relevant to me. I care a lot about doing things well, and that can come out as intensity before people know that I actually care about them too.
entries.reflection: I can get very focused on getting something done well. The Trailblazers feedback conversation showed me that being direct can still make people feel pushed aside. I am working on asking more questions, making more space, and giving feedback in a way that helps people feel supported.

entries.title: The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo
entries.principle: Craft & Share a Compelling Vision
entries.left_note: I have thought about this book many times while writing scholarship essays, preparing for interviews, and building this project. It is strange to tell your own story while knowing that every version leaves something out.
entries.reflection: Evelyn made me think about the difference between controlling a narrative and being clear about what you stand for. I do not need a perfect version of my story. I want people to see the real themes in it: creativity, education, meaningful work, and showing up for people.

entries.title: Normal People
entries.principle: Cultivate Self-Awareness, Personal Agility & Growth
entries.left_note: I love this book because it is quiet, but it is also frustrating in the most recognizable way. So much happens because people assume the other person already knows what they mean or how they feel.
entries.reflection: This book reminds me that it is not enough to know my own strengths and weaknesses privately. People need to understand where I am coming from too. That matters in teams as much as it does in relationships. I am trying to say things more clearly instead of assuming my intent is obvious.

entries.title: The Hunger Games
entries.principle: Actively Find & Formulate the Right Problems
entries.left_note: I first read this when I was younger, mostly because I could not put it down. Reading it again after Trailblazers, I noticed how the story keeps changing the question in front of you.
entries.reflection: Katniss starts by trying to survive the problem right in front of her. The story slowly shows that the real problem is much bigger than the Games. That connects to strategic leadership for me. The first issue you see may not be the root issue. I need to look at the systems, incentives, and people behind a problem before I get attached to a solution.

entries.title: Educated
entries.principle: Cultivate Self-Awareness, Personal Agility & Growth
entries.left_note: I remember finishing this book and feeling like it made growth feel less polished than people usually talk about it. Becoming more yourself can also mean letting go of things that once made sense to you.
entries.reflection: Growth can be uncomfortable, especially when it asks you to rethink something you once felt sure about. That is why I value feedback even when it is hard to hear. I want to stay open to people and experiences that challenge the assumptions I bring into a room.

entries.title: Punching the Air
entries.principle: Maintain a Relentless Focus on Creating Value
entries.left_note: This is one of the books that made me pause more than once because it is written in verse. It makes Amal’s voice feel so immediate, which is exactly why it is hard to look away from what happens to him.
entries.reflection: Amal’s voice and creativity stay important even when a system tries to reduce him to one story about who he is. The book makes me think about whose stories are believed, heard, and valued. When I work with people, I want to notice who is left out of the conversation and whose perspective is easiest to miss.

entries.title: The Invisible Life of Addie LaRue
entries.principle: Maintain a Relentless Focus on Creating Value
entries.left_note: This book is probably the most magical one on this shelf, but what has stayed with me is actually a pretty practical question: what does it mean to make a mark when no one is keeping score?
entries.reflection: Addie’s life made me think about the things we create and the people we affect when no one is keeping score. I want my work to be useful to people. That matters more to me than choosing something that simply looks impressive on paper.

entries.title: Project Hail Mary
entries.principle: Identify & Align Resources to Generate Value
entries.left_note: I picked this because it is fun and weird and unexpectedly emotional, but also because Rocky and Ryland are such a good reminder that collaboration does not require people to think or work the same way.
entries.reflection: The main character cannot solve the problem by being smart on his own. He has to experiment, adapt, and work with someone who thinks very differently from him. That feels connected to the product and team work I want to do. I want to stay curious about strengths that are different from mine and build better things with other people.
